title: Chapter 90 — Heads or Tails
paragraphs: "De balena vero sufficit, si rex habeat caput, et regina caudam." — Bracton, l. 3, c. 3.

Latin from the books of the Laws of England, which, read in context, means that of all whales caught by anyone on the coast of that country, the King, as Honorary Grand Harpooner, must get the head, and the Queen must respectfully be given the tail. With a whale, this division is a lot like cutting an apple in half: nothing is left over in between. Now, since this law, in a modified form, is still in force in England today, and since it presents in several ways a strange exception to the general law of Fast and Loose-Fish, it gets a chapter of its own here — on the same courteous principle that leads the English railways to go to the expense of a separate car reserved especially for royalty. First, as a curious proof that the law just mentioned is still in force, let me put before you something that happened within the last two years.

It seems that some honest sailors of Dover, or Sandwich, or some one of the Cinque Ports, had after a hard chase succeeded in killing and beaching a fine whale which they had originally spotted far off from the shore. Now the Cinque Ports are partially or somehow under the jurisdiction of a sort of policeman or beadle (a minor parish officer) called a Lord Warden. He holds the office directly from the crown, I believe, and all the royal revenues from the Cinque Port territories become his by assignment. Some writers call this office a sinecure. But not so. Because the Lord Warden is busily employed at times in pocketing his perquisites — which are his chiefly by virtue of that same pocketing of them.

Now when these poor sun-burnt sailors, barefoot and with their trousers rolled high up on their eel-like legs, had wearily hauled their fat fish high and dry, promising themselves a good £150 from the precious oil and bone — and in their imaginations already sipping fine tea with their wives and good ale with their friends, upon the strength of their respective shares — up steps a very learned and most Christian and charitable gentleman, with a copy of Blackstone under his arm. Laying it upon the whale's head, he says: "Hands off! This fish, my masters, is a Fast-Fish. I seize it as the Lord Warden's." Upon this, the poor sailors in their respectful consternation — so truly English — knowing not what to say, fell to vigorously scratching their heads all round, meanwhile ruefully glancing from the whale to the stranger. But that did nothing to mend the matter or soften the hard heart of the learned gentleman with his copy of Blackstone. At length one of them, after long scratching about for his ideas, made bold to speak:
"Please, sir, who is the Lord Warden?"
"The Duke."
"But the Duke had nothing to do with taking this fish?"
"It is his."
"We have been at great trouble and peril and some expense, and is all that to go to the Duke's benefit — we getting nothing at all for our pains but our blisters?"
"It is his."
"Is the Duke so very poor as to be forced to this desperate way of getting a livelihood?"
"It is his."
"I meant to help support my old bedridden mother with part of my share of this whale."
"It is his."
"Won't the Duke be content with a quarter or a half?"
"It is his."

In short, the whale was seized and sold, and his Grace the Duke of Wellington got the money. Feeling that, seen in certain lights, the case might just possibly, and in some small degree, be considered rather a hard one under the circumstances, an honest clergyman of the town wrote his Grace a respectful note, begging him to give the case of those unlucky sailors his full consideration. To this my Lord Duke replied, in substance (both letters were published), that he had already done so, and had received the money, and would be obliged to the reverend gentleman if in future he (the reverend gentleman) would kindly refrain from meddling with other people's business. Is this the still-militant old man who stands at the corners of the three kingdoms, forcing alms out of beggars on every side?

It is easy to see that in this case the Duke's claimed right to the whale was one delegated to him by the Sovereign. So we have to ask on what principle the Sovereign holds that right in the first place. The law itself has already been stated. But Plowdon gives us the reason for it. According to Plowdon, a whale caught this way belongs to the King and Queen "because of its superior excellence." And the soundest commentators have always considered this a compelling argument in such matters.
But why should the King get the head and the Queen the tail? Give us a reason for that, you lawyers!

In his treatise on "Queen-Gold," or Queen's pin-money, an old King's Bench author, one William Prynne, writes thus: "The tail is the Queen's, that the Queen's wardrobe may be supplied with whalebone." Now this was written at a time when the black limber bone of the Greenland or right whale was widely used in ladies' bodices. But this same bone is not in the tail; it is in the head — which is a sad mistake for a learned lawyer like Prynne. But is the Queen a mermaid, to be presented with a tail? An allegorical meaning may lurk here.

English legal writers name two royal fish — the whale and the sturgeon — both of them royal property within certain limits, and in name supplying the tenth branch of the crown's ordinary revenue. I am not aware that any other author has touched on the matter, but it seems to me by inference that the sturgeon must be divided the same way as the whale, the King getting that fish's peculiarly dense and elastic head — which, taken symbolically, may possibly be humorously grounded in some supposed kinship. And so there seems to be a reason for everything, even in law.
